newsitem.title: CHINA: Strong Hong Kong to Europe air cargo mkt expected.
newsitem.headline: Strong Hong Kong to Europe air cargo mkt expected.

text.p: Freight forwarders face a hike in air cargo rates between Hong Kong and major European destinations as the market emerges from its traditional slack season, a Reuters survey showed.

Major airlines anticipating that the peak season is imminent, have already sent out notices warning of a HK$3 per kg rate rise from August 1 as they expect the market to continue strengthening as demand for space rises.
Of the two major air cargo markets from Hong Kong, that to the U.S. has been the first to boom but the hope is Europe will not be far behind.
"The carriers are obviously hoping the peak season is just around the corner which is why they are all raising rates," said one well known forwarder.
"The European market is slowly picking up but is still far from booming. However, since last weekend, space has become tighter which is a sure sign that the market is changing," he added.
In a year which has followed traditional patterns, predictions for when the peak season will begin varied with middle of August the preferred choice.
A spokesman for Hellman International Forwarders Ltd expected the market to Europe to start matching current peak demand to the U.S. early in August judging by bookings for space already received.
"The last few weeks have been quiet but congestion will increase in the coming weeks for sure," he said.
For some carriers, the peak has started early.
British Airways World Cargo said it is enjoying load factors of more than 90 per cent on its three leased freighters between Hong Kong and the UK.
"Traffic to the UK is on the way up and the slack season is now history. We now don't have to worry about filling our aircraft," said BA's area cargo manager, Chris Chan.

Chan said the trans-Pacific market is currently booming and taking precedence over the European market but once manufacturers fulfill U.S. needs, demand for space aboard Europe-bound flights will similarly take off.
Like other carriers to Europe, BA has already informed customers of an August one HK$3 per kg rate rise.

BA's passenger and cargo flights between London and Hong Kong were unaffected by recent industrial action which affected other Asian routes and cost the airline dear. The cancellation of two ex-Hong Kong passenger flights in the aftermath of the strike because of crew shortages had a minimal effect on cargo throughput, Chan added.

BA's outlook for the rest of the peak season in the run-up to Christmas was optimistic with UK importers reporting high levels of orders being placed with Hong Kong and southern Chinese firms instead of with Vietnamese or Indonesian ones as has been the recent trend.
"Prospects are good for the rest of the year," Chan said.

Lufthansa Cargo, which dominates the market to Frankfurt with its joint venture with Cathay Pacific Airways offering 11 Boeing 747 freighters a week against nine a year ago, was also looking forward to a good second half.

"The peak season is starting now but it will build up and become busier during August. Our customers tell us that they expect healthy exports from Hong Kong to Europe for the latter part of the year. I think it will be a good second half of the year," reported a Lufthansa cargo spokesman.
The market had been performing to expectations with a weak May and June "but is now picking up nicely. We are happy with the way things have worked out," he added.
Like many other carriers, Lufthansa said rates had remained relatively stable during the slack season, unlike last year when they sank to memorably low levels.

Ex-Hong Kong average rates for small shipments to London Heathrow were reported to range between HK$20-24 per kilo, depending on the airline involved and the routing. Discounts were available for larger loads.
Generally, airline spokesmen said the slow season, which is now coming to an end had not affected business or rate levels as dramatically as in previous years.
European carriers also said they were benefitting from a booming U.S. market which is keeping rival Asian carriers more focussed on trans-Pacific traffic.
"They are carrying so much U.S. bound traffic that they can't cope with European bound traffic too which is good news for us," reported one major European based airline.

Another complained of "impossibly" low rate levels being offered by some airlines and singled out Thailand's flag carrier, Thai Airways International, as selling up to 30 per cent below average market rates. A Thai spokesman in Hong Kong was unavailable for comment.
"They simply cannot be making a profit. They must make a loss, because we have one of the lowest cost structures in the industry and we can't compete," said one airline manager.

Anthony Lau, the chairman of the 261 member Hong Kong Association of Freight Forwarding Agents Ltd who is also chairman and chief executive of BALtrans Holdings said trade to Europe is not yet as strong as to the U.S.

That opinion was shared by South Korea's Asiana Airlines which reported high loads ex-Hong Kong to Seoul and good business on its Boeing 747 Combi flights to its European destinations: Vienna, Brussels and Frankfurt. Asiana also operates a weekly B747-400 service to Amsterdam.

"The slow season is almost finished and it is already the peak season which will last until the end of the year. Rates have also been rising," the spokesman said, although he declined to detail by how much.
South Korean flag carrier Korean Air Lines also reported reduced loads to Europe destinations compared with its major market, the U.S.

Emirates, which operates seven weekly passenger flights between Hong Kong and Dubai as well as two wet-leased freighter services, said there were signs the market was reviving but did not expect it to start to peak until later in August.

"On past experience the market should pick up around the middle of July but this year it seems a little slow. The market is stronger than May and June but is still not substantial because of overcapacity in the market. But the expectations are good for August and we think the market will be able to sustain the planned rate rise," reported Jacky Lau, Emirates' Hong Kong cargo manager.
Flights from Dubai to Europe were currently busier than from Hong Kong to Dubai, Lau added.
Emirates, which stressed it was a "premium carrier" because of its levels of service, was reported to have the highest Hong Kong to Dubai cargo selling rate at between HK$16-18 per kilo.
Recalling last year, when rates dropped to an all time low, industry spokesmen said rates this year have remained relatively steady through the traditional slack season of May and June.
Airline sources said they were keen to avoid last year's criticism from shippers of too many rate rises too often, including two within three weeks.
"It is easier for shippers to handle one or two rises spread over a period of time, we realise that this year," said one.
Forwarding agents generally said because margins have been low they expect to pass most of the HK$3 rate rise onto their customers.

"The market this year is better than last year and the airlines are taking the opportunity to raise rates. If they raise their rates we will have to raise ours and pass it on to our customers. We will be able to absorb some but not the major part," said a spokesman for Burlington Air Express.

Aviation analysts have identified sizeable increases in cargo carrying capacity on ex-Hong Kong routes to Europe being achieved by major airlines such as Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd which has recently been allowed to fly a new shorter route over China.

Scandinavian Airlines Systems has also added capacity with a third weekly Boeing 747 freighter between Gothenburg and Macau. A large proportion of its cargo originates in Hong Kong and goes by barge to Macau.

Russia's privatised Transaero Airlines has joined Aeroflow in offering an alternative Moscow service with a weekly DC-10 with 10 tonnes of belly capacity. - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
